claim: Fast spiking, parvalbumin (PV) expressing hippocampal interneurons are classified into basket, axo-axonic (chandelier), and bistratified cells.
source: Fast spiking, parvalbumin (PV) expressing hippocampal interneurons are classified into basket, axo-axonic (chandelier), and bistratified cells.
evidence: This is a statement of established classification in the field, supported by scientific consensus.

claim: During slower (<10 Hz) theta oscillations, each PV cell class exhibited its own characteristic, relatively uniform firing behavior.
source: During the slower (<10 Hz) theta oscillations, each cell class exhibited its own characteristic, relatively uniform firing behavior.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental observations presented in the manuscript.

claim: During faster (>90 Hz) oscillations, within-class differences in PV interneuron discharges emerged, which segregated along specific features of dendritic structure or somatic location.
source: However, during faster (>90 Hz) oscillations, within-class differences in PV interneuron discharges emerged, which segregated along specific features of dendritic structure or somatic location.
evidence: This is a primary finding supported by experimental data presented in the manuscript.

claim: Functional divergence of PV sub-classes during fast but not slow network oscillations effectively doubles the repertoire of spatio-temporal patterns of GABA release available for rapid circuit operations.
source: Functional divergence of PV sub-classes during fast but not slow network oscillations effectively doubles the repertoire of spatio-temporal patterns of GABA release available for rapid circuit operations.
evidence: This is an interpretive conclusion based on the experimental findings.

claim: Brain state-dependent network oscillations occurring at various frequencies provide multiscale temporal windows for the precise timing of neuronal discharges and the temporal binding of spatially distributed cell populations.
source: Brain state-dependent network oscillations occurring at various frequencies provide multiscale temporal windows for the precise timing of neuronal discharges and the temporal binding of spatially distributed cell populations (Singer, 1993; Buzsaki and Chrobak, 1995).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: The spatio-temporal control of principal cell assemblies during endogenous brain rhythms is orchestrated by GABAergic interneurons.
source: The spatio-temporal control of principal cell assemblies during endogenous brain rhythms is orchestrated by GABAergic interneurons (Soltesz, 2006; Somogyi et al., 2014).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: Within the CA1 region of the rodent hippocampus, 21 distinct interneuronal classes are currently recognized.
source: Within the CA1 region of the rodent hippocampus, 21 distinct interneuronal classes are currently recognized, each possessing unique input–output connectivity patterns, developmental profiles, and characteristic molecular and electrophysiological properties (Klausberger and Somogyi, 2008; Bezaire and Soltesz, 2013).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: Parvalbumin expressing (PV) interneurons serve major mechanistic roles in a variety of network functions, including local circuit operations, learning and memory, rhythmogenesis, sensory processing, and critical period plasticity.
source: The parvalbumin expressing (PV) interneurons, in particular, have been identified to serve major mechanistic roles in a variety of network functions, including local circuit operations, learning and memory, rhythmogenesis, sensory processing, and critical period plasticity (Pouille and Scanziani, 2004; Buzsaki and Wang, 2012; Kuhlman et al., 2013; Siegle and Wilson, 2014).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: PV cells have been linked to a number of neurological and psychiatric disorders including epilepsy, schizophrenia, and autism.
source: Furthermore, PV cells have also been linked to a number of neurological and psychiatric disorders including epilepsy, schizophrenia, and autism (Lewis et al., 2005; Ogiwara et al., 2007; Gibson et al., 2009; Armstrong and Soltesz, 2012; Verret et al., 2012; Trouche et al., 2013).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: PV cells can fire fast action potentials at high frequencies with little accommodation.
source: A key property of PV cells is speed; indeed, these interneurons can fire fast action potentials at high frequencies with little accommodation (Kawaguchi, 1995; Buhl et al., 1996)
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: PV cells possess fast membrane time constants.
source: indeed, these interneurons can fire fast action potentials at high frequencies with little accommodation (Kawaguchi, 1995; Buhl et al., 1996), possess fast membrane time constants
evidence: This is a known property of PV cells from the literature.

claim: PV cells release GABA with high temporal precision following the arrival of presynaptic action potentials at the release sites.
source: possess fast membrane time constants, and release GABA with high temporal precision following the arrival of presynaptic action potentials at the release sites, enabling PV cells to serve as the rapid signaling elements of interneuronal–principal cell networks (Bartos et al., 2001; Jonas et al., 2004; Hu et al., 2010).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: PV cells sharply segregate into three major classes that are differentiated based on the distinct post-synaptic domains that they innervate.
source: Importantly, PV cells are known to sharply segregate into three major classes that are differentiated based on the distinct post-synaptic domains that they innervate (Klausberger and Somogyi, 2008).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to previous literature.

claim: Axo-axonic (chandelier) cells (AACs) make synaptic contacts exclusively on the axon initial segments of principal cells.
source: Axo-axonic (chandelier) cells (AACs) make synaptic contacts exclusively on the axon initial segments of principal cells (Somogyi, 1977; Somogyi et al., 1983).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: Basket cells (BCs) innervate the somata and proximal dendrites of the target cells.
source: In contrast, basket cells (BCs) innervate the somata and proximal dendrites of the target cells
evidence: This is established knowledge about BC anatomy.

claim: Bistratified (Bistrat) cells provide GABAergic inputs to the basal and apical dendritic domains.
source: whereas the bistratified (Bistrat) cells provide GABAergic inputs to the basal and apical dendritic domains (Buhl et al., 1994).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to previous literature.

claim: To date only a single AAC has been reported from the CA1 region under non-anesthetized in vivo conditions.
source: For example, although AACs have received a lot of attention as playing major roles in the synchronization of principal cell populations (Howard et al., 2005; Szabadics et al., 2006; Woodruff et al., 2010), to date only a single AAC has been reported from the CA1 region under non-anesthetized in vivo conditions (Viney et al., 2013).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to previous literature.

claim: There are no data on the preferential phase-specific discharges of AACs and Bistrat cells during high-frequency (>90 Hz) oscillations in vivo in awake animals.
source: Similarly, in spite of a series of recent studies examining anatomically and immunocytochemically identified (Lapray et al., 2012; Varga et al., 2012; Viney et al., 2013; Katona et al., 2014) or optogenetically 'tagged' interneurons in vivo without anesthesia (Royer et al., 2012; Kvitsiani et al., 2013), there are no data on the preferential phase-specific discharges of AACs and Bistrat cells during high-frequency (>90 Hz) oscillations in vivo in awake animals.
evidence: This claim identifies a gap in the literature based on review of previous studies.

claim: A total of 27 fast spiking PV interneurons were post-hoc identified, comprising 12 BCs, 8 Bistrat cells, and 7 AACs.
source: Fast spiking PV interneurons (total: n = 27; Figure 1A) were post-hoc identified primarily based on their axonal characteristics as BCs (n = 12; 7 were included in Varga et al., 2012), Bistrat cells (n = 8), or AACs (n = 7).
evidence: This is a direct report of the experimental sample size.

claim: Axons of the BCs were largely confined to the stratum pyramidale, where they formed synapses on the somata and proximal dendrites of PCs.
source: Axons of the BCs were largely confined to the stratum pyramidale, where they formed synapses on the somata and proximal dendrites of PCs.
evidence: This is based on anatomical observations from the recorded cells.

claim: Electron microscopic verification of somatic axonal targets of BCs was performed in n = 4 cells.
source: Electron microscopic verification of somatic axonal targets of BCs was performed in n = 4 cells.
evidence: This is a direct report of the experimental verification method.

claim: Bistratified cells had the majority of their axons in the stratum radiatum and some in the stratum oriens.
source: In contrast, the dendritically projecting Bistrat cells had the majority of their axons in the stratum radiatum and some in the stratum oriens.
evidence: This is based on anatomical observations from the recorded cells.

claim: The axons of Bistrat cells avoided the stratum pyramidale.
source: Since the axons of Bistrat cells avoided the stratum pyramidale, the axons provided a feature of Bistrat cells that clearly distinguished them from the other two cell classes.
evidence: This is based on anatomical observations from the recorded cells.

claim: The targets of n = 5 AACs were identified at the EM level, with all examined boutons synapsing on axon initial segments.
source: The targets of n = 5 AACs were identified at the EM level (number of boutons examined: 11, 10, 10, 8, 4, all synapsing on axon initial segments).
evidence: This is a direct report of electron microscopy verification results.

claim: PV immunopositivity was confirmed in 8 out of the 8 tested BCs.
source: Specifically, PV immunopositivity was confirmed in 8 out of the 8 tested BCs
evidence: This is a direct report of immunohistochemical verification results.

claim: PV immunopositivity was confirmed in 3 out of the 5 tested Bistrat cells.
source: PV immunopositivity was confirmed in 8 out of the 8 tested BCs, 3 out of the 5 tested Bistrat cells
evidence: This is a direct report of immunohistochemical verification results.

claim: PV immunopositivity was confirmed in 3 out of the 3 tested AACs.
source: PV immunopositivity was confirmed in 8 out of the 8 tested BCs, 3 out of the 5 tested Bistrat cells, and 3 out of the 3 tested AACs.
evidence: This is a direct report of immunohistochemical verification results.

claim: SOM immunopositivity was verified in all 8 out of the 8 tested Bistrat cells.
source: SOM immunopositivity was verified in all 8 out of the 8 tested Bistrat cells
evidence: This is a direct report of immunohistochemical verification results.

claim: SOM expression distinguishes Bistrat cells from BCs and AACs.
source: SOM immunopositivity was verified in all 8 out of the 8 tested Bistrat cells, which is important since SOM expression distinguishes Bistrat cells from BCs and AACs (Klausberger and Somogyi, 2008).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to previous literature.

claim: Bistrat cells have been observed to exhibit generally weaker PV immunoreactivity compared to BCs.
source: Note that Bistrat cells have been observed to exhibit generally weaker PV immunoreactivity compared to BCs (Ferraguti et al., 2004)
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to previous literature.

claim: Theta oscillations (5 Hz–10 Hz), gamma (25 Hz–90 Hz), and epsilon (90 Hz–130 Hz) oscillations were studied during running.
source: Accordingly, theta (5 Hz–10 Hz), gamma (25 Hz–90 Hz), and epsilon (90 Hz–130 Hz) oscillations were studied during running
evidence: This is a direct statement of the experimental design.

claim: Ripples (90 Hz–200 Hz) occurred during rest.
source: whereas ripples (90 Hz–200 Hz) occurred during rest.
evidence: This is a direct statement of the experimental design.

claim: Epsilon oscillations reflect network events generated locally in CA1.
source: Specifically, epsilon oscillations reflect network events generated locally in CA1 (Schomburg et al., 2014)
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to previous literature.

claim: Most pyramidal cells (PCs) show strong phase locking to the trough of the epsilon oscillations.
source: and most pyramidal cells (PCs) show strong phase locking to the trough of the epsilon oscillations, indicating large synchrony of PC discharges during these events (Belluscio et al., 2012; Schomburg et al., 2014).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: The three distinct PV cell classes discharged at comparable frequencies during theta.
source: The three distinct cell classes discharged at comparable frequencies during theta (Figure 1B,D–F; AAC: 27.1 ± 9.1 Hz, n = 5; BC: 28.64 ± 9.4 Hz, n = 12; Bistrat: 34.03 ± 11.9 Hz, n = 8; p = 0.84, one way ANOVA).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data and statistical analysis.

claim: Every PV cell showed theta modulation of its firing (p < 0.001 for all cells, Rayleigh test).
source: While every cell showed theta modulation of its firing (p < 0.001 for all cells, Rayleigh test)
evidence: This claim is supported by statistical analysis of experimental data.

claim: AACs showed the most prominent theta modulation, followed by the intermediate level of modulation of the BCs, whereas Bistrat cells were only weakly modulated.
source: Specifically, AACs showed the most prominent theta modulation, followed by the intermediate level of modulation of the BCs, whereas Bistrat cells were only weakly modulated (Figure 1D–F).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental observations shown in the figures.

claim: Statistical analysis revealed significant differences in the strength of theta modulation between the three cell classes (AACs: r = 0.44 ± 0.1; BCs: r = 0.25 ± 0.1; Bistrat cells: r = 0.17 ± 0.05; p < 0.01; Kruskal–Wallis test).
source: Statistical analysis of the strength of theta modulation of action potential discharges revealed significant differences between the three cell classes (modulation strength, from the highest to low: AACs: r = 0.44 ± 0.1; BCs: r = 0.25 ± 0.1; Bistrat cells: r = 0.17 ± 0.05; p < 0.01; Kruskal–Wallis test; Figure 1C).
evidence: This claim is supported by statistical analysis of experimental data.

claim: The AACs preferred the middle of the descending phase of theta (251° ± 17°).
source: The AACs preferred the middle of the descending phase (251° ± 17°; 0° is considered to be the trough, 180° the peak of the individual oscillatory cycle).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data on phase-preferential firing.

claim: AACs did not preferentially fire close to the theta peak during running, as they were reported to do so under anesthesia.
source: Thus, AACs did not preferentially fire close to the theta peak during running, as they were reported to do so under anesthesia (Klausberger et al., 2003).
evidence: This claim compares current findings with previous literature under different conditions.

claim: BCs fired on average during the late descending phase of theta (310° ± 23°).
source: The preferential discharges of the AACs during the theta cycle were followed by the BCs that fired on average during the late descending phase (310° ± 23°)
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data on phase-preferential firing.

claim: Bistrat cells discharged near the trough of theta (0° ± 17°), around the time that the mean preferential discharges of most PCs take place.
source: while Bistrat cells discharged near the trough (0° ± 17°), around the time that the mean preferential discharges of most PCs take place (Mizuseki et al., 2011).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data and comparison with previous literature.

claim: The different PV interneuron classes deliver GABA in a sequential manner along the long (axon initial segment–somato-dendritic) axis of the CA1 PCs.
source: These data suggest that the different PV interneuron classes deliver GABA in a sequential manner along the long (axon initial segment–somato-dendritic) axis of the CA1 PCs
evidence: This is an interpretation based on the phase-preferential firing data.

claim: The bulk of spatio-temporally organized inhibition sweeps through the PC populations from the axon initial segment to the dendrites within about 40 ms during running-associated theta.
source: and that the bulk of this spatio-temporally organized inhibition sweeps through the PC populations from the axon initial segment to the dendrites within about 40 ms during running-associated theta (calculated for an average, 8 Hz theta rhythm).
evidence: This is a calculation based on the phase differences observed in the data.

claim: The BC, AAC, and Bistrat cell groups occupied different parts of the phase vs modulation strength plot.
source: The BC, AAC, and Bistrat cell groups occupied different parts of the phase vs modulation strength plot (Figure 1C)
evidence: This is an observation from the data visualization.

claim: There was a high degree of within-class uniformity in how members of the three cell groups discharged during theta oscillations.
source: As illustrated in Figure 1C for the AACs, BCs, and Bistrat cells, there was a high degree of within-class uniformity in how members of these three cell groups discharged during theta oscillations.
evidence: This is an observation from the data visualization.

claim: Extracellularly recorded fast spiking single units without direct anatomical identification cannot be unambiguously classified as belonging to one of the three PV cell classes based on the theta-related firing alone.
source: Therefore, extracellularly recorded fast spiking single units (e.g., recorded with tetrodes or silicon probes) without direct anatomical identification cannot be unambiguously classified as belonging to one of these three cell classes based on the theta-related firing alone, even if the unit is identified as expressing PV (e.g., with optogenetic tagging; [Royer et al., 2012]).
evidence: This is an inference based on the overlap observed in the phase vs modulation strength plot.

claim: Gamma oscillations are thought to play important roles in information transfer between brain areas.
source: Gamma oscillations are thought to play important roles in information transfer between brain areas (Engel and Singer, 2001; Womelsdorf et al., 2007; Sirota et al., 2008; Atallah and Scanziani, 2009)
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: Perisomatic inhibition is mechanistically important in the generation of gamma-frequency oscillations.
source: there is an overall agreement that perisomatic inhibition is mechanistically important in the generation of gamma-frequency oscillations (Buzsaki and Wang, 2012).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to previous literature.

claim: Gamma oscillations appear during the falling phase of the running-associated theta rhythm.
source: Gamma oscillations appear during the falling phase of the running-associated theta rhythm (see peak gamma activity centered around 60 Hz in Figure 2A).
evidence: This is an observation from the time-frequency analysis shown in the figure.

claim: Not all PV cells fired in a gamma-modulated manner (number of cells significantly modulated: BCs: 9/12; Bistrat cells: 6/8; AACs: 4/5).
source: Interestingly, although fast spiking PV cells are important in gamma oscillations (Buzsaki and Wang, 2012), not all PV cells in our recordings fired in a gamma-modulated manner (number of cells significantly modulated: BCs: 9/12; Bistrat cells: 6/8; AACs: 4/5).
evidence: This is a direct report of experimental observations.

claim: The modulation strength of gamma firing was only moderate and there was no difference between the perisomatically (BCs, AACs) vs dendritically (Bistrat cells) projecting PV interneurons (BC: r = 0.18 ± 0.07; Bistrat cells: r = 0.18 ± 0.05; AAC: r = 0.17 ± 0.08; p = 0.79; Kruskal–Wallis test).
source: Furthermore, the modulation strength was only moderate (in agreement with Tukker et al., 2007; Varga et al., 2012), and there was no difference between the perisomatically (BCs, AACs) vs dendritically (Bistrat cells) projecting PV interneurons in terms of the strength of modulation (BC: r = 0.18 ± 0.07; Bistrat cells: r = 0.18 ± 0.05; AAC: r = 0.17 ± 0.08; p = 0.79; Kruskal–Wallis test).
evidence: This claim is supported by statistical analysis of experimental data and comparison with previous literature.

claim: BCs preferentially fired during the middle ascending phase of the individual gamma waves (110 ± 18°), significantly earlier than the other two cell classes (p < 0.01; Watson–Williams test).
source: BCs preferentially fired during the middle ascending phase of the individual gamma waves (110 ± 18°), significantly earlier than the other two cell classes (p < 0.01; Watson–Williams test)
evidence: This claim is supported by statistical analysis of experimental data.

claim: Bistrat cells discharged on average during the late ascending phase of gamma (148 ± 23°).
source: that discharged on average during the late ascending phase (Bistrat cells: 148 ± 23°)
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data on phase-preferential firing.

claim: AACs discharged close to the peak of the gamma oscillations (181 ± 15.4°).
source: or close to the peak of the gamma oscillations (AACs: 181 ± 15.4°).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data on phase-preferential firing.

claim: The majority of cells in each PV class was moderately modulated by gamma-frequency oscillations.
source: These data indicate that the majority of cells in each PV class was moderately modulated by gamma-frequency oscillations
evidence: This is a summary interpretation of the experimental findings.

claim: BCs preferentially fired earlier during the individual gamma waves compared to either the Bistrat cells or the AACs.
source: and that the BCs preferentially fired earlier during the individual gamma waves compared to either the Bistrat cells or the AACs.
evidence: This is a summary interpretation of the experimental findings.

claim: Epsilon oscillations occurred during the second half of the falling phase of the running-associated theta waves.
source: The epsilon oscillations occurred during the second half of the falling phase of the running-associated theta waves (asterisk in Figure 2A).
evidence: This is an observation from the time-frequency analysis shown in the figure.

claim: AACs were either not epsilon modulated (n = 3) or they exhibited only weak epsilon modulation (n = 2; r = 0.19 and 0.12).
source: Indeed, AACs were either not epsilon modulated (n = 3) or they exhibited only weak epsilon modulation (n = 2; blue triangles in Figure 2C; r = 0.19 and 0.12; y-axis in Figure 2C).
evidence: This is a direct report of experimental observations.

claim: The firing probabilities of every BC and Bistrat cell showed significant epsilon modulation.
source: In contrast to AACs, the firing probabilities of every BC and Bistrat cell showed significant epsilon modulation (Figure 2C).
evidence: This is a direct report of experimental observations.

claim: On average, the modulation strength of the BCs was higher than that of the Bistrat cells during epsilon (BC: r = 0.38 ± 0.09, Bistrat: r = 0.26 ± 0.07; p < 0.01, Mann–Whitney test).
source: On average, the modulation strength of the BCs was higher than that of the Bistrat cells (BC: r = 0.38 ± 0.09, Bistrat: r = 0.26 ± 0.07; p < 0.01, Mann–Whitney test).
evidence: This claim is supported by statistical analysis of experimental data.

claim: The more precise epsilon-related firing activity of BCs compared to Bistrat cells (and AACs) likely contributes to the regulation of PC discharges during epsilon epochs.
source: These data indicate a more precise epsilon-related firing activity of BCs compared to Bistrat cells (and AACs), which likely contributes to the regulation of PC discharges during epsilon epochs (Belluscio et al., 2012; Schomburg et al., 2012).
evidence: This is an interpretation based on the experimental findings and previous literature.

claim: BCs on average fired significantly earlier during the epsilon waves compared to the Bistrat cells (BCs: 66 ± 17°, n = 12; Bistrat cells: 126 ± 14°, n = 8; p < 0.001; Watson–Williams test; 1–1.5 ms delay).
source: The BCs on average fired significantly earlier during the epsilon waves compared to the Bistrat cells (BCs: 66 ± 17°, n = 12; Bistrat cells: 126 ± 14°, n = 8; p < 0.001; Watson–Williams test; 1–1.5 ms delay)
evidence: This claim is supported by statistical analysis of experimental data.

claim: The 2 significantly epsilon-modulated AACs preferentially fired at phases similar to Bistrat cells (137° and 108°).
source: the 2 significantly epsilon-modulated AACs preferentially fired at phases similar to Bistrat cells (137° and 108°; Figure 2C).
evidence: This is a direct report of experimental observations.

claim: The firing of PV interneurons segregates according to the three established major PV cell classes during epsilon oscillations that take place when the animal is running.
source: Taken together, these data show that the firing of PV interneurons segregates according to the three established major PV cell classes during epsilon oscillations that take place when the animal is running.
evidence: This is a summary interpretation of the experimental findings.

claim: The rest-associated high-frequency oscillations have at least an order of magnitude higher increase in power than the running-associated epsilon oscillations.
source: In fact, the rest-associated high frequency oscillations have at least an order of magnitude higher increase in power than the running-associated epsilon oscillations (compare the heat-colored, Z-scored power above 90 Hz in Figure 2A vs Figure 2D).
evidence: This is an observation from the time-frequency analysis shown in the figures.

claim: Ripples represent one of the fastest (up to 200 Hz, lasting approximately 40 ms–150 ms) and most synchronized episodic electrographic events in the normal brain.
source: Ripples, which are known to be associated with sharp-waves in the CA1 area (O'Keefe and Nadel, 1978; Buzsaki et al., 1983), represent one of the fastest (up to 200 Hz, lasting approximately 40 ms–150 ms; for an example, see Figure 3) and most synchronized episodic electrographic events in the normal brain (Buzsaki, 1986)
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous literature and observations from the current study.

claim: Ripples are crucial for memory consolidation by replaying the encoded ensemble firing patterns in a time-compressed manner.
source: and are crucial for memory consolidation by replaying the encoded ensemble firing patterns in a time-compressed manner (Wilson and McNaughton, 1994; Foster and Wilson, 2006).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: BCs discharged at a high rate (77 ± 28 Hz) during ripple events, dramatically increasing their discharge probability.
source: In agreement with previous reports (Lapray et al., 2012; Katona et al., 2014), BCs discharged at a high rate (77 ± 28 Hz) during ripple events, dramatically increasing their discharge probability (Figure 2E).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data and comparison with previous literature.

claim: Bistrat cells significantly increased their discharge probabilities during ripples, but their firing frequency was about half of that of the BCs during the ripple events (36 ± 16 Hz, p < 0.01 with respect to BCs, Mann–Whitney).
source: Bistrat cells also significantly increased their discharge probabilities during ripples, but their firing frequency was about half of that of the BCs during the ripple events (36 ± 16 Hz, p < 0.01 with respect to BCs, Mann–Whitney; Figure 2E).
evidence: This claim is supported by statistical analysis of experimental data.

claim: AACs on average, as a group (n = 7), showed no significant changes in firing rates during ripple events.
source: In contrast to BCs and Bistrat cells, the AACs on average, as a group (n = 7), showed no significant changes in firing rates during ripple events (blue line in Figure 2E).
evidence: This is a direct report of experimental observations.

claim: AACs fired the majority (68.3 ± 17.3%, n = 7) of their ripple-related spikes during the beginning of the ripple events (before the ripple reached its maximal amplitude).
source: Further analysis showed that the AACs fired the majority (68.3 ± 17.3%, n = 7) of their ripple-related spikes during the beginning of the ripple events (before the ripple reached its maximal amplitude), in broad agreement with the discharge dynamics noted by Klausberger et al., 2003.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data and comparison with previous literature.

claim: The ripple-related modulation strengths of the firing of BCs and Bistrat cells were high and not different from each other (BCs: r = 0.63 ± 0.12; Bistrat: r = 0.62 ± 0.08).
source: The ripple-related modulation strengths of the firing of BCs and Bistrat cells were high and not different from each other (BCs: r = 0.63 ± 0.12; Bistrat: r = 0.62 ± 0.08).
evidence: This is a direct report of experimental observations.

claim: Bistrat cells were weakly modulated during the running-associated epsilon waves but strongly modulated during the rest-associated ripples.
source: Therefore, Bistrat cells were weakly modulated during the running-associated epsilon waves but strongly modulated during the rest-associated ripples (Figure 2C,F).
evidence: This is a summary interpretation comparing findings across different oscillations.

claim: BCs on average discharged significantly earlier than the Bistrat cells during ripples (55 ± 20° vs 126 ± 10°, p < 0.001, Watson–Williams test).
source: In terms of phase-preferential firing during ripples, the BCs on average discharged significantly earlier than the Bistrat cells (55 ± 20° vs 126 ± 10°, p < 0.001, Watson–Williams test)
evidence: This claim is supported by statistical analysis of experimental data.

claim: There was a sharp division between the two clusters representing the BCs and the Bistrat cells in the phase vs modulation strength plot during ripples.
source: with a sharp division between the two clusters representing the BCs (red circles) and the Bistrat cells (green squares) in the phase vs modulation strength plot in Figure 2F.
evidence: This is an observation from the data visualization.

claim: BCs discharged on virtually every ripple event (95 ± 6%).
source: Our analysis revealed that BCs discharged on virtually every ripple event (in agreement with [Varga et al., 2012]), whereas Bistrat cells remained silent (Figure 3A,B) on about a third of the ripple episodes (percentage of ripple events when the interneurons fired: BCs: 95 ± 6%
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data and comparison with previous literature.

claim: Bistrat cells remained silent on about a third of the ripple episodes (68 ± 13%).
source: whereas Bistrat cells remained silent (Figure 3A,B) on about a third of the ripple episodes (percentage of ripple events when the interneurons fired: BCs: 95 ± 6%; Bistrat cells: 68 ± 13%; p < 0.01, Mann–Whitney).
evidence: This claim is supported by statistical analysis of experimental data.

claim: Whether or not a Bistrat cell fired during a ripple correlated with the oscillation frequency of the individual ripple events.
source: Furthermore, the data showed that whether or not a Bistrat cell fired during a ripple correlated with the oscillation frequency of the individual ripple events (i.e., with the intra-ripple or 'core' frequency of the LFP oscillations; these are highlighted in red in the example traces in Figure 3A,B).
evidence: This is a direct report of experimental observations.

claim: The core frequency of the ripples when Bistrat cells discharged was significantly higher than the core frequency of those ripples during which the Bistrat cells did not discharge (mean core frequency of ripple events without Bistrat cell spikes: 122.5 ± 18 Hz, n = 191 events; with spikes: 140 ± 17 Hz, 347 events; n = 8 cells, p < 0.0001, Mann–Whitney test).
source: Namely, as illustrated in Figure 3C,D, the core frequency of the ripples when Bistrat cells discharged was significantly higher than the core frequency of those ripples during which the Bistrat cells did not discharge (mean core frequency of ripple events without Bistrat cell spikes: 122.5 ± 18 Hz, n = 191 events; with spikes: 140 ± 17 Hz, 347 events; n = 8 cells, p < 0.0001, Mann–Whitney test).
evidence: This claim is supported by statistical analysis of experimental data.

claim: Bistrat cells differentiate between lower vs higher frequency ripple events, in sharp contrast to BCs.
source: Therefore, these results indicate that, in sharp contrast to BCs (Figure 3B,D), Bistrat cells (Figure 3A,C) differentiate between lower vs higher frequency ripple events
evidence: This is an interpretation based on the experimental findings.

claim: Rest-associated high-frequency events showed no evidence of a bimodal distribution with a minimum at 140 Hz.
source: (note that, as illustrated in the inset in Figure 3D, rest-associated high-frequency events in our recordings showed no evidence of a bimodal distribution with a minimum at 140 Hz, the frequency boundary used to separate high gamma and ripple events in sleeping or awake immobile rats [see Figure 1B in Sullivan et al., 2011]).
evidence: This is an observation from the data analysis shown in the figure inset.

claim: Both the epsilon- and the ripple-associated discharges of PV interneurons display characteristic properties that segregate along previously established class lines.
source: Taken together, these data show that both the epsilon- and the ripple-associated discharges of PV interneurons display characteristic properties that segregate along previously established class lines.
evidence: This is a summary interpretation of the experimental findings.

claim: The phase-specific discharges of BCs characteristically preceded Bistrat cell firing during fast oscillations (>90 Hz), regardless of the behavioral state of the animal (epsilon during running, ripples during rest).
source: Furthermore, these results demonstrate that the phase-specific discharges of BCs characteristically preceded Bistrat cell firing during fast oscillations (>90 Hz), regardless of the behavioral state of the animal (epsilon during running, ripples during rest).
evidence: This is a summary interpretation of the experimental findings.

claim: One sub-class of Bistrat cells (C-Bistrat) has extensive dendrites both in the oriens and the radiatum layers, with the dendrites in the stratum radiatum extending up to the border with the lacunosum-moleculare layer.
source: One sub-class has extensive dendrites both in the oriens and the radiatum layers, with the dendrites in the stratum radiatum extending up to the border with the lacunosum-moleculare layer (Klausberger et al., 2004; Katona et al., 2014)
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: C-Bistrat cells presumably receive inputs both from the local CA1 PCs and the Schaffer collateral/commissural inputs from the CA3 PCs.
source: which presumably allows these cells to receive inputs both from the local CA1 PCs and the Schaffer collateral/commissural inputs from the CA3 PCs (note that axons from CA3 PCs are present in the CA1 stratum oriens as well [Sik et al., 1993; Wittner et al., 2006]).
evidence: This is a speculation based on anatomical considerations and previous literature.

claim: O-Bistrat cells have their entire dendritic tree confined to the stratum oriens with no dendrites in the stratum radiatum.
source: In contrast, other Bistrat cells have their entire dendritic tree confined to the stratum oriens with no dendrites in the stratum radiatum (Maccaferri et al., 2000)
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to previous literature.

claim: From the n = 8 Bistrat cells, 3 were C-Bistrat and 5 were O-Bistrat cells.
source: From our n = 8 Bistrat cells, 3 were C-Bistrat (Figure 4A,C and 5) were O-Bistrat cells (Figure 4B,C).
evidence: This is a direct report of the experimental sample composition.

claim: Both Bistrat sub-classes provided dense axonal projections to the radiatum, with minor innervation of the oriens layers.
source: Note that both sub-classes provided dense axonal projections to the radiatum, with minor innervation of the oriens layers (Figure 4A,B).
evidence: This is an observation from the anatomical reconstructions.

claim: There was no difference in the running-associated theta-related firing of C- and O-Bistrat cells (firing frequency during theta: O-Bistrat: 34.6 ± 14.7 Hz; C-Bistrat: 27.2 ± 6.5 Hz; p = 0.67, Mann–Whitney).
source: Indeed, there was no difference in the running-associated theta-related firing of C- and O-Bistrat cells in our sample either (firing frequency during theta: O-Bistrat: 34.6 ± 14.7 Hz; C-Bistrat: 27.2 ± 6.5 Hz; p = 0.67, Mann–Whitney; Figure 4D
evidence: This claim is supported by statistical analysis of experimental data.

claim: During rest-associated ripples, O-Bistrat cells fired significantly faster than C-Bistrat cells (O-Bistrat: 44.2 ± 11.0 Hz; C-Bistrat: 19.8 ± 3.7 Hz; p = 0.035, Mann–Whitney).
source: In contrast, during rest-associated ripples, O-Bistrat cells fired significantly faster than C-Bistrat cells (O-Bistrat: 44.2 ± 11.0 Hz; C-Bistrat: 19.8 ± 3.7 Hz; p = 0.035, Mann–Whitney; Figure 4E)
evidence: This claim is supported by statistical analysis of experimental data.

claim: The different firing rates of the O-Bistrat and C-Bistrat cell sub-classes during ripples demonstrate the emergence of intra-class functional differences among Bistrat cells during fast network oscillations.
source: The different firing rates of the O-Bistrat and C-Bistrat cell sub-classes during ripples demonstrate the emergence of intra-class functional differences among Bistrat cells during fast network oscillations.
evidence: This is an interpretation based on the experimental findings.

claim: O-Bistrat cells had especially high firing frequencies during ripples, suggesting that dendrites in the radiatum are not required for elevated levels of discharges in these cells during ripple events.
source: In addition, the fact that O-Bistrat cells had especially high firing frequencies during ripples suggests that dendrites in the radiatum are not required for elevated levels of discharges in these cells during ripple events.
evidence: This is an interpretation based on the experimental findings.

claim: 2 out of the 5 AACs for whom theta, gamma, and epsilon-related firing could be analyzed showed significant modulation of action potential discharges during running-associated epsilon waves.
source: One potential clue was our observation that, as mentioned above, 2 out of the 5 AACs for whom theta, gamma, and epsilon-related firing could be analyzed showed significant modulation of action potential discharges during running-associated epsilon waves (Figure 2C)
evidence: This is a direct report of experimental observations.

claim: The somata of five AACs were situated within the PC layer or at the PC layer and stratum oriens border (C-AACs).
source: Indeed, we noted that the somata of five of our AACs were situated within the PC layer or at the PC layer and stratum oriens border (Figure 5A,C; we refer to these cells as Classical or C-AACs)
evidence: This is a direct report of anatomical observations.

claim: The somata of two AACs that showed epsilon-modulation were located outside of the PC layer (E-AACs).
source: whereas the somata of the two AACs that showed epsilon-modulation were located outside of the PC layer (Figure 5B,D; we refer to these cells as External or E-AACs. Such E-AACs have been also noted before [Ganter et al., 2004; Forro et al., 2013]).
evidence: This is a direct report of anatomical observations and comparison with previous literature.

claim: C-AACs either did not alter (4 out of 5) or decrease (1 out of 5) their firing rates during ripples.
source: As illustrated in Figure 5E,G, C-AACs either did not alter (4 out of 5) or decrease (1 out of 5) their firing rates during ripples (inset in Figure 5G).
evidence: This is a direct report of experimental observations.

claim: The two E-AACs significantly increased their discharge rates during ripples (from 5.6 Hz–23 Hz, and from 3.8 Hz–7.5 Hz; p < 0.001 for each cell).
source: In sharp contrast to the C-AACs, the two E-AACs significantly increased their discharge rates during ripples (Figure 5F,H; from 5.6 Hz–23 Hz, and from 3.8 Hz–7.5 Hz; p < 0.001 for each cell).
evidence: This claim is supported by statistical analysis of experimental data.

claim: The strength of modulation of the ripple-related firing by the E-AACs was strong (r = 0.69 and r = 0.45), comparable to that of the BCs and Bistrat cells.
source: Furthermore, the strength of modulation of the ripple-related firing by the E-AACs was strong (r = 0.69 and r = 0.45; blue triangles in Figure 2F), comparable to that of the BCs and Bistrat cells.
evidence: This is a direct report of experimental observations.

claim: This is the first in vivo evidence of a sub-population of AACs enhancing their discharge probabilities during ripple oscillations.
source: Apart from in vitro reports (Hajos et al., 2013), to our knowledge, this is the first in vivo evidence of a sub-population of AACs enhancing their discharge probabilities during ripple oscillations
evidence: This is a claim about the novelty of the finding based on review of the literature.

claim: E-AACs showed preferred phases of firing during ripples comparable to Bistrat cells (mean phase values for the E-AACs: 115° and 124°).
source: Interestingly, the E-AACs showed preferred phases of firing during ripples comparable to Bistrat cells (Figure 2F; mean phase values for the E-AACs: 115° and 124°
evidence: This is a direct report of experimental observations.

claim: E-AACs also showed similar phase values to Bistrat cells during the epsilon oscillations.
source: note that the E-AACs also showed similar phase values to Bistrat cells during the epsilon oscillations as well; Figure 2C).
evidence: This is a direct report of experimental observations.

claim: 5 out of the 5 C-AACs and 1 out of the 2 E-AACs showed significantly decreased probability of firing in the immediate post-ripple period.
source: Additionally, it is worthwhile to note that while only one of the AACs decreased its firing during the ripples, 5 out of the 5 C-AACs and 1 out of the 2 E-AACs showed significantly decreased probability of firing in the immediate post-ripple period (see Figure 5G).
evidence: This is a direct report of experimental observations.

claim: Similar post-ripple decrease in firing was reported previously for C-AACs from anesthetized rats.
source: Similar post-ripple decrease in firing was reported previously for C-AACs from anesthetized rats (Klausberger et al., 2003).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to previous literature.

claim: There is a functional splitting of the AAC class during fast network events.
source: Therefore, these observations demonstrate that there is a functional splitting of the AAC class during fast network events as well, in addition to the differences described above for the ripple-related discharges of the Bistrat cell sub-classes.
evidence: This is an interpretation based on the experimental findings.

claim: BC somata have been reported to be occasionally located outside the stratum pyramidale.
source: Indeed, BC somata have been reported to be occasionally located outside the stratum pyramidale (Pawelzik et al., 2002)
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to previous literature.

claim: No functional differences have been reported between BCs situated inside vs outside the cell layer.
source: but no functional differences have been reported between BCs situated inside vs outside the cell layer.
evidence: This is a statement about the absence of previous findings in the literature.

claim: Among the n = 12 successfully recorded and post-hoc visualized BCs, there were three cells with cell bodies and dendrites exclusively in the stratum oriens (H-BCs).
source: Among our n = 12 successfully recorded and post-hoc visualized BCs, there were three cells with cell bodies and dendrites exclusively in the stratum oriens (Figure 6B).
evidence: This is a direct report of anatomical observations.

claim: All three H-BCs were positive for PV and targeted somata.
source: All of these three cells were positive for PV (Figure 6E) and targeted somata (Figure 6F; number of boutons examined that synapsed on somata: n = 9; dendrites: n = 3; target unidentified: n = 2).
evidence: This is a direct report of immunohistochemical and electron microscopy verification results.

claim: H-BCs had axonal projections into (n = 2) or towards (n = 1) the subiculum.
source: We refer to these BCs with somata and dendrites in the oriens as horizontal or H-BCs (note that H-BCs had axonal projections into [n = 2] or towards [n = 1] the subiculum).
evidence: This is a direct report of anatomical observations.

claim: C-BCs had vertically oriented dendrites that spanned across the oriens to the radiatum, with branches extending into the lacunosum-moleculare layer.
source: The H-BCs were clearly distinct from their more canonical counterparts (referred to as classical or C-BCs below), whose somata were located within the PC layer and the C-BCs had vertically oriented dendrites that spanned across the oriens to the radiatum, with branches extending into the lacunosum-moleculare layer (Figure 6A).
evidence: This is a direct report of anatomical observations.

claim: H-BCs often fired two spikes per individual ripple cycle (doublets of action potentials), which occurred only rarely in C-BCs.
source: Importantly, analysis showed that the morphologically distinct BC sub-classes displayed differential firing behavior during fast network oscillations. Namely, H-BCs often fired two spikes per individual ripple cycle (i.e., doublets of action potentials) (Figure 6H), which occurred only rarely in C-BCs (Figure 6G).
evidence: This is a direct report of experimental observations.

claim: H-BCs also fired more intensely during ripples.
source: In addition, H-BCs also fired more intensely during ripples (Figure 6H).
evidence: This is a direct report of experimental observations.

claim: The proportion of ripples when the cells fired doublets of action potentials was significantly different between H-BCs and C-BCs (H-BCs: 77.9 ± 11.6%; C-BCs: 17.3 ± 12%; p = 0.009, Mann–Whitney).
source: Quantification of the firing patterns of the two BC sub-classes showed statistical differences both in terms of the proportion of ripples when the cells fired doublets of action potentials (Figure 6I; H-BCs: 77.9 ± 11.6%; C-BCs: 17.3 ± 12%; p = 0.009, Mann–Whitney)
evidence: This claim is supported by statistical analysis of experimental data.

claim: The average firing frequency during the ripples was significantly different between H-BCs and C-BCs (H-BCs: 128.9 ± 23.8 Hz; C-BCs: 62.7 ± 12.3 Hz; p = 0.004, Mann–Whitney).
source: and in terms of the average firing frequency during the ripples (Figure 6J; H-BCs: 128.9 ± 23.8 Hz; C-BCs: 62.7 ± 12.3 Hz; p = 0.004, Mann–Whitney).
evidence: This claim is supported by statistical analysis of experimental data.

claim: Intra-class differences in firing behavior during fast network oscillations also existed for the BCs, similar to what was described for the Bistrat cells and the AACs.
source: Taken together, these results showed that intra-class differences in firing behavior during fast network oscillations also existed for the most numerically dominant PV interneuronal class, the BCs, similar to what was described above for the Bistrat cells and the AACs.
evidence: This is a summary interpretation of the experimental findings.

claim: AACs fired with the strongest theta modulation among the three PV cell classes.
source: The data showed that the AACs fired with the strongest theta modulation.
evidence: This is a summary of experimental findings.

claim: The one AAC previously reported from the CA1 of non-anesthetized freely moving rats discharged at 225° during theta.
source: Although inter-species differences cannot be ruled out, the one AAC previously reported from the CA1 of non-anesthetized freely moving rats in the literature also discharged well after the theta peak (at 225°) (Viney et al., 2013).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to previous literature.

claim: All of the 20 optogenetically tagged PV cells in a recent study conducted in freely moving mice discharged during the descending phase of the theta rhythm and none fired preferentially at the peak.
source: Furthermore, it is interesting to note that all of the 20 optogenetically tagged PV cells in a recent study conducted in freely moving mice discharged during the descending phase of the theta rhythm and none fired preferentially at the peak (Royer et al., 2012).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to previous literature.

claim: In animals during running, the axon initial segments of PCs receive a barrage of GABA inputs from AACs during the descending phase of the theta cycle (at 251° on average), followed by inputs from BCs onto their cell bodies and proximal dendrites about 20 ms later (at 310°), and then, with another approximately 20 ms delay on average, near the theta trough (360° or 0°), Bistrat cells release GABA onto the basal and mid-level apical dendrites.
source: Therefore, it appears that in animals during running, the axon initial segments of PCs receive a barrage of GABA inputs from AACs during the descending phase of the theta cycle (at 251° on average), followed by inputs from BCs onto their cell bodies and proximal dendrites about 20 ms later (at 310°), and then, with another approximately 20 ms delay on average, near the theta trough (360° or 0°), Bistrat cells release GABA onto the basal and mid-level apical dendrites.
evidence: This is an interpretation based on the experimental findings.

claim: The pattern of discharges by the three cardinal PV interneuron classes is organized to generate a spatio-temporally exquisitely orchestrated axon initial segment to somata/proximal dendrites to mid-level dendrites sweep of fast GABAergic inhibition in a relatively short time window.
source: Thus, the pattern of discharges by the three cardinal PV interneuron classes is organized to generate a spatio-temporally exquisitely orchestrated axon initial segment to somata/proximal dendrites to mid-level dendrites sweep of fast GABAergic inhibition in a relatively short time window (Figure 7A, 'Theta').
evidence: This is an interpretation based on the experimental findings.

claim: BCs clearly differed from Bistrat cells and AACs in their strong modulation by epsilon oscillations.
source: First, BCs clearly differed from Bistrat cells and AACs in their strong modulation by epsilon oscillations.
evidence: This is a summary of experimental findings.

claim: Somatic and proximal dendritic GABAergic inputs from BCs may play primary roles in shaping the excitability of PCs during epsilon-associated behaviors.
source: These results indicate that somatic and proximal dendritic GABAergic inputs from BCs may play primary roles in shaping the excitability of PCs during epsilon-associated behaviors.
evidence: This is an interpretation based on the experimental findings.

claim: BCs as a group differed from the Bistrat cell and AAC classes in exhibiting the highest rates of firing during ripple events.
source: Second, BCs as a group also differed from the Bistrat cell and AAC classes in exhibiting the highest rates of firing during ripple events.
evidence: This is a summary of experimental findings.

claim: Marked differences were found between Bistrat cell and BC discharges during ripples with low core frequencies, indicating that Bistrat cell-derived dendritic inhibition is only recruited during high-frequency sharp-wave ripple events.
source: Third, we found marked differences between Bistrat cell and BC discharges during ripples with low core frequencies, indicating that Bistrat cell-derived dendritic inhibition is only recruited during high-frequency sharp-wave ripple events.
evidence: This is an interpretation based on the experimental findings.

claim: BCs on average fired earlier than Bistrat cells and AACs during all network oscillations faster than the theta range, including the running-associated, theta-embedded gamma and epsilon waves, as well as sharp-wave ripples during rest.
source: Fourth, our data revealed that BCs on average fired earlier than Bistrat cells and AACs during all network oscillations faster than the theta range, including the running-associated, theta-embedded gamma and epsilon waves, as well as sharp-wave ripples during rest (Figure 7A).
evidence: This is a summary of experimental findings.

claim: The finding of BCs firing earlier than Bistrat cells and AACs during fast oscillations indicates a behavioral state-independent leadership position (primacy) of BCs in interneuronal firing sequences during fast oscillatory cycles.
source: The latter finding indicates a behavioral state-independent leadership position (referred to as primacy below) of BCs in interneuronal firing sequences during fast oscillatory cycles
evidence: This is an interpretation based on the experimental findings.

claim: A frequency-invariant temporal ordering of BC and oriens-moleculare interneuron (OLM cells) discharges was previously observed, where the preferred phases of firing of BCs were significantly earlier than the mean phase of discharges by the OLM cells during both epsilon and ripple events.
source: extending our previous observations of a frequency-invariant temporal ordering of BC and oriens-moleculare interneuron (OLM cells project to the distal dendritic regions of CA1 PCs) discharges, where the preferred phases of firing of BCs were also significantly earlier than the mean phase of discharges by the OLM cells during both epsilon and ripple events (Varga et al., 2012).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to previous literature.

claim: AACs in awake mice, when considered together as a single group, exhibited no significant changes in firing rates during ripple events, fired the majority of their spikes at the beginning of the ripples, and decreased their firing in the immediate post-ripple period, in overall agreement with data from anesthetized rats.
source: In addition to these four major inter-class differences during fast network oscillations, our data also showed that AACs in awake mice, when considered together as a single group, exhibited no significant changes in firing rates during ripple events, fired the majority of their spikes at the beginning of the ripples, and decreased their firing in the immediate post-ripple period, in overall agreement with data from anesthetized rats (Klausberger et al., 2003).
evidence: This is a summary of experimental findings and comparison with previous literature.

claim: AACs in the CA1 do not necessarily stop delivering GABA during ripple events when sub-sets of PCs are known to replay previously experienced firing sequences.
source: Therefore, AACs in the CA1 do not necessarily stop delivering GABA during ripple events when sub-sets of PCs are known to replay previously experienced firing sequences (Wilson and McNaughton, 1994; O'Neill et al., 2008, 2010)
evidence: This is an interpretation based on the experimental findings and previous literature.

claim: AACs may actively regulate PC discharges during sharp-wave ripples.
source: indicating that AACs may actively regulate PC discharges during sharp-wave ripples.
evidence: This is a speculation based on the experimental findings.

claim: Robust intra-class distinctions emerged from all three major PV cell classes during fast (>90 Hz), but not slow, network oscillations.
source: Importantly, in addition to inter-class differences between PV cells, our data also revealed that robust intra-class distinctions emerged from all three major PV cell classes during fast (>90 Hz), but not slow, network oscillations (Figure 7B).
evidence: This is a summary of experimental findings.

claim: Differences in somatic layer position, in conjunction with significant physiological differences, qualify distinct AACs and BCs as separate, novel interneuronal sub-classes.
source: Differences in somatic layer position, in conjunction with significant physiological differences, qualify these distinct AACs and BCs as separate, novel interneuronal sub-classes (note that layer-specific location together with differential spiking behaviors in vivo was also used as the basis of the differentiation of a previously unified cell class into neurogliaform and ivy cell sub-classes [Fuentealba et al., 2008]).
evidence: This is an interpretation based on the experimental findings and comparison with previous literature.

claim: The newly identified differentially discharging PV sub-classes are likely to be not negligible in terms of their abundance, as the population of PV interneurons in the stratum oriens has been estimated to be about 30% of the number of PV cells within the stratum pyramidale.
source: Importantly, these newly identified differentially discharging PV sub-classes are likely to be not negligible in terms of their abundance, as the population of PV interneurons in the stratum oriens has been estimated to be about 30% of the number of PV cells within the stratum pyramidale (in 1000s: BCs: 1.3/3.9; Bistrat cells: 0.5/1.6; AACs: 0.3/1) (Bezaire and Soltesz, 2013).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to previous literature.

claim: The H-BC/C-BC and E-AAC/C-AAC ratios (3/10 and 2/5, respectively) in the sample approximated 30%, indicating that the oriens layer cells were not under-sampled.
source: Reassuringly, the H-BC/C-BC and E-AAC/C-AAC ratios (3/10 and 2/5, respectively) in our sample approximated 30%, indicating that we did not under-sample the oriens layer cells.
evidence: This is an interpretation based on the experimental sample composition.

claim: Potential differences between intrinsic excitability and excitatory and inhibitory connectivity may contribute to the differences in firing frequencies of the new PV sub-classes during fast rhythms in the CA1.
source: Future studies will be needed to identify the reasons for the differences in firing frequencies of these new PV sub-classes during fast rhythms in the CA1, but they may include potential differences between intrinsic excitability (e.g., as reported for fast spiking BCs and AACs in the neocortex and CA3) (Woodruff et al., 2009; Papp et al., 2013) and excitatory and inhibitory connectivity (Hajos et al., 2013) both from within the CA1 as well as from extrinsic sources (e.g., AACs have been reported to receive differential inhibitory innervation from the septum [Viney et al., 2013]).
evidence: This is a speculation about future research directions based on previous literature.

claim: BCs are known to synapse not only on PCs but also on the other PV expressing cells as well.
source: One clue to this question may be related to the fact that BCs are known to synapse not only on PCs but also on the other PV expressing cells as well (Cobb et al., 1997).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to previous literature.

claim: BC axons are largely confined to the stratum pyramidale.
source: A second potential clue is that BC axons are largely confined to the stratum pyramidale (Glickfeld and Scanziani, 2006; Foldy et al., 2007)
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: PV cells whose cell bodies and proximal dendrites are located outside the PC layer will be in a privileged position to escape inhibition from BCs.
source: thus, PV cells whose cell bodies and proximal dendrites are located outside the PC layer will be in a privileged position to escape inhibition from BCs.
evidence: This is a logical inference based on the anatomical properties of BCs.

claim: The average phase-preferential discharges of Bistrat cells, and the two epsilon and ripple-modulated AACs, were delayed by about 1.4 ms (calculated for a 140-Hz ripple) with respect to the mean phase of firing by BCs during fast network events, a period of time that is approximately a monosynaptic delay.
source: A third relevant point is that our data showed that the average phase-preferential discharges of Bistrat cells, and the two epsilon and ripple-modulated AACs in our sample, were delayed by about 1.4 ms (calculated for a 140-Hz ripple) with respect to the mean phase of firing by BCs during fast network events, a period of time that is approximately a monosynaptic delay.
evidence: This is a calculation based on the experimental data.

claim: Firing of BCs early during each ripple cycle is expected to deliver synaptic inhibition to other BCs as well as to AACs and Bistrat cells.
source: Therefore, firing of BCs early during each ripple cycle is expected to deliver synaptic inhibition to other BCs as well as to AACs and Bistrat cells.
evidence: This is a logical inference based on the connectivity and timing of BC firing.

claim: Although BCs are known to be able to fire at 100s of Hz with little or no accommodation, most BCs fired only a single spike per ripple cycle.
source: Indeed, although BCs are known to be able to fire at 100s of Hz with little or no accommodation (Kawaguchi, 1995; Buhl et al., 1996), most BCs fired only a single spike per ripple cycle.
evidence: This is an observation from the experimental data and comparison with previous literature.

claim: The exceptions to BCs firing only a single spike per ripple cycle were precisely those BCs whose cell bodies were outside of the PC layer (the H-BCs), which discharged at higher intra-ripple frequencies and fired frequent doublets during ripple cycles.
source: The exceptions were precisely those BCs whose cell bodies were outside of the PC layer (and thus largely outside of the BC axonal cloud) the H-BCs, which discharged at higher intra-ripple frequencies and fired frequent doublets during ripple cycles (Figure 7B).
evidence: This is an interpretation based on the experimental findings.

claim: The early firing of BCs is expected to inhibit the later-discharging AACs and Bistrat cells as well, likely contributing to their relatively lower frequencies of firing during ripples.
source: The early firing of BCs is expected to inhibit the later-discharging AACs and Bistrat cells as well, likely contributing to their relatively lower frequencies of firing during ripples.
evidence: This is a speculation based on the connectivity and timing of BC firing.

claim: AACs whose cell bodies are outside of the PC body layer would be predicted to be able to largely escape the BC-derived inhibition, which is consistent with the observation that such E-AACs significantly increased their firing rates during ripple events.
source: However, AACs whose cell bodies are outside of the PC body layer would be predicted to be able to largely escape the BC-derived inhibition, which is consistent with our observation that such E-AACs significantly increased their firing rates during ripple events (Figure 7B).
evidence: This is an interpretation based on the experimental findings.

claim: The early firing of BCs during fast network events is likely to differentially regulate the excitability of those interneurons whose cell bodies are located inside vs outside the termination zone of BC axons.
source: While future studies will be needed to identify the precise factors shaping the temporal ordering of interneuronal discharges, the early firing of BCs during fast network events is likely to differentially regulate the excitability of those interneurons whose cell bodies are located inside vs outside the termination zone of BC axons.
evidence: This is a speculation based on the experimental findings.

claim: The database of PV cells presented in this paper is the largest collection of anatomically and immunocytochemically identified fast-spiking cells that have been recorded from non-anesthetized animals in vivo to date.
source: Nevertheless, even though only a single cell was attempted to be juxtacellularly labeled in each animal, the database of PV cells presented in this paper is the largest collection of anatomically and immunocytochemically identified fast-spiking cells that have been recorded from non-anesthetized animals in vivo to date.
evidence: This is a claim about the significance of the dataset based on review of the literature.

claim: Interneurons are estimated to be 38,500/349,500 or about 11% of the total CA1 neuron population.
source: Interneurons are a minority (estimated to be 38,500/349,500 or about 11%) of the total CA1 neuron population
evidence: This claim is supported by established knowledge from the literature.

claim: PV cells comprise approximately a quarter of the interneurons in the CA1 (9200/38,500, 23.9%).
source: and PV cells comprise approximately a quarter of the interneurons in the CA1 (9200/38,500, 23.9%) (Bezaire and Soltesz, 2013).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to previous literature.

claim: Among the PV cell classes, BCs are estimated to be the most numerous (14% of all CA1 interneurons), followed by the Bistrat cells (6%) and the AACs (4%).
source: Among the PV cell classes, BCs are estimated to be the most numerous (14% of all CA1 interneurons), followed by the Bistrat cells (6%) and the AACs (4%) (Baude et al., 2007; Bezaire and Soltesz, 2013).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: The frequencies of occurrence of the three PV cell classes in the database (n = 12 BCs; n = 8 Bistrat cells; n = 5 AACs) roughly matched the ratio expected from the literature, indicating a lack of a major sampling bias.
source: Reassuringly, these frequencies of occurrence roughly matched the ratio of the cell numbers for the three PV cell classes in our database (n = 12 BCs; n = 8 Bistrat cells; n = 5 AACs), indicating a lack of a major sampling bias for the various PV cell classes in our juxtacellular recordings.
evidence: This is an interpretation based on comparison of the experimental sample with literature estimates.

claim: An advantage of the head-fixed juxtacellular recording approach is that the mice under head-fixed conditions produce relatively long periods of running (typically tens of seconds), which allows robust sampling of continuous theta rhythm and the associated theta-nested epsilon oscillations while maintaining high-quality juxtacellular recordings from single cells.
source: Although recordings from head-fixed animals have certain limitations (e.g., in studies of eye movements) (Wallace et al., 2013), an advantage of the head-fixed juxtacellular recording approach (Varga et al., 2012) for the study of network oscillations is that the mice under head-fixed conditions produce relatively long periods of running (typically tens of seconds), which allows robust sampling of continuous theta rhythm and the associated theta-nested epsilon oscillations while maintaining high-quality juxtacellular recordings from single cells.
evidence: This is a discussion of the advantages of the experimental approach.

claim: Theta-related juxtacellular recordings from non-head-fixed freely moving but tethered and spatially confined rats were reportedly limited to short periods of head movements and postural shifts while the animals remained in the same location.
source: In contrast, theta-related juxtacellular recordings from non-head-fixed freely moving but tethered and spatially confined rats were reportedly limited to short periods of head movements and postural shifts while the animals remained in the same location (Viney et al., 2013)

claim: Caution has to be exercised when trying to infer precise interneuronal identity from extracellular unit data, even if combined with optogenetic tagging.
